newsitem.title: zaire: Mobutu to leave Zaire Wednesday, says will return.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu to leave Zaire Wednesday, says will return.

text.p: Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko, under pressure to resign as rebels close in on Kinshasa, will travel to Gabon on Wednesday and return to the capital two days later, his spokesman said on Tuesday.
"It is confirmed that the president will go to Libreville on Wednesday and will return on Friday. He is attending a meeting of heads of state," spokesman Kabuya Lumuna told Reuters.
"The meeting is linked to the international mediation on Zaire," Kabuya said.

The announcement came as Laurent Kabila's rebels, who were reportedly less than 85 km (50 miles) from the city of five million, appealed for government troops to surrender to their approaching forces to avert a bloody takeover of the capital.

Rebel radio said the rebels had ringed the airport outside Kinshasa and were about to take the whole city. There was no independent confirmation of the rebel claim and a Reuters journalist in the area said there was no sign of rebel troops.
Similar claims in the past have often proved to be exaggerated or wrong.
In announcing Mobutu's trip, Kabuya gave no details about which presidents would meet in the capital of Gabon, whose President Omar Bongo has been on close terms with Mobutu for three decades.

A presidential aide said earlier it would be wrong to interpret Mobutu's departure as a flight into exile, recalling that the 66-year-old president, now suffering from prostate cancer, has always said he will not flee the city.
The rebel campaign to oust Mobutu, who has ruled for 32 years, began last October.

The surrender appeal by the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire said rebels had set up centres to receive government troops and would not harm those willing to turn themselves in.
"A surrender is important because it will avoid bloodshed in Kinshasa," said the statement issued in the name of the rebel military high command.

Kinshasa residents were slow to venture onto the normally busy streets on Tuesday. In the commercial district scores of people, hungry for the latest news, clustered around newspaper vendors -- avidly reading newspapers spread on the ground.
Many Kinshasa residents openly welcome the prospect of Kabila's arrival but fear Mobutu's soldiers will again loot and pillage before fleeing.
American envoy Bill Richardson kept up his diplomatic shuttle across southern Africa, flying to Cape Town from Botswana for further talks to avert a battle for the capital.
U.S. official sources in Cape Town said Richardson was heading directly for talks with South Africa's deputy president, Thabo Mbeki.

In the past week, President Bill Clinton's envoy has held talks with Mobutu, Kabila and the leaders of most of Zaire's nine African neighbours, which would be threatened by the collapse of the vast central African state.
Earlier on Tuesday in Botswana, Richardson met Ugandan leader Yoweri Museveni, Zimbabwe's President Robert Mugabe and Tanzania's Benjamin Mkapa.
In Paris, longtime Mobutu ally France expressed deep concern over rebel threats to take Kinshasa by force if necessary and renewed its appeals for a peaceful transition.

United Nations and Organisation of African Unity special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was in Paris for talks with officials at President Jacques Chirac's office and the foreign ministry, ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.
Rummelhardt said France would renew support for Sahnoun's peace plan during the talks and discuss the summit held between Mobutu and Kabila at the weekend.
